title: Rebounding and the lymphatic system
summary: How lymph moves without a heart pump, why mini-trampoline bouncing is discussed for drainage, what research actually shows, and how to practice rebounding if you own a rebounder.

sections.heading: The lymphatic system has no central pump
sections.body: Blood circulation has the heart; lymph does not. Lymph collects between cells, enters thin-walled capillaries, and travels through nodes before returning to the bloodstream near the collarbones. Movement is essential: skeletal muscle contractions, breathing, and arterial pulsation create pressure changes that push lymph through one-way valves. Long stillness slows that passive pumping—one reason lymphatic flow shows up as a lifestyle variable.

sections.heading: What rebounding is
sections.body: Rebounding usually means rhythmic bouncing on a mini-trampoline (rebounder) with a flexible mat—often gentle, feet staying on the surface, knees slightly bent. It is low-impact compared with hard-surface running. Sessions are often short (5–15 minutes). Quality rebounders have stable frames; cheap toy trampolines are not the same safety class. Because it requires equipment, this guide treats rebounding as optional—you only practice it if you own a rebounder.

sections.heading: Why people link bouncing to lymph flow
sections.body: The popular argument is mechanical: each landing creates a brief load-and-release cycle. Proponents say rhythmic vertical acceleration acts like an external pump. Mainstream physiology agrees that muscle activity and pressure gradients move lymph; the debated part is whether rebounding is uniquely superior to walking, swimming, yoga, or resistance training. Rebounding may simply be an efficient, joint-friendly way to get repetitive loading—useful if you will actually do it.

sections.heading: What research does and does not show
sections.body: Exercise science has studied mini-trampoline training for balance, fitness, and adherence—often with modest positive results. Direct imaging of lymph flow during rebounding is sparse compared with clinical lymphedema care (manual drainage, compression, complete decongestive therapy). Those clinical tools are evidence-based for specific diagnoses; recreational rebounding is not a substitute. Honest summary for healthy people: rebounding is real exercise that moves muscle and increases breathing—facts that support lymph transport physiologically. “Detox” toxin-load claims overshoot the literature.

sections.heading: Where Dr. Jack Kruse’s teaching is specific
sections.body: Kruse’s public material often highlights rebounding as a mitochondrial lifestyle tool for lymphatic “waste” clearance and cellular water turnover—nested inside light–water–magnetism (daylight movement, cold, grounding, less sedentary indoor time). He tends to prescribe short daily rebound sessions more strongly than generic “exercise more.” Those integrated claims are his framework layer. Mainstream medicine agrees sedentary behavior impairs fluid movement; it does not universally endorse rebounding over other modalities.

sections.heading: What is solid, what is framework
sections.body: Solid ground: lymph needs movement; exercise raises breathing and muscle pump; unexplained swelling needs clinical evaluation before aggressive bouncing. Framework: that a few minutes on a rebounder uniquely detoxes quantified toxin loads or replaces medical lymphedema care. Unexplained limb swelling, post-lymph-node surgery, or radiation history → see a clinician first.

sections.heading: How to use it here
sections.body: Practice Exercise → Rebounding (or the rebounding path your build exposes), then outdoors or indoors, then duration. Soft bounces, both feet down, posture tall. Outdoor rebounding stacks movement with daylight. If you do not own equipment, use walking or bands instead. Educational only—not medical advice for lymphedema or post-operative care.
